solution:
The two columns interlock: each blank is the mirror of the entry facing it. Completed chart —

| Asexual reproduction | Sexual reproduction |
|---|---|
| 1. Reproduction that occurs with the help of somatic cells is called as asexual reproduction. | 1. **Reproduction that occurs with the help of gametes (germ cells) is called as sexual reproduction.** |
| 2. **Only one parent is necessary for asexual reproduction; it is uniparental reproduction.** | 2. Male and female parent are necessary for sexual reproduction. |
| 3. This reproduction occurs with the help of mitosis only. | 3. **This reproduction occurs with the help of both meiosis and mitosis — gametes are formed by meiosis and the zygote then divides by mitosis.** |
| 4. **New individual formed by this method has exact genetic similarity with the reproducing organism.** | 4. New individual formed by this method is genetically different from parents. |
| 5. Asexual reproduction occurs in different individuals by various methods like binary fission, multiple fission, budding, fragmentation, regeneration, vegetative propagation, spore production, etc. | 5. **Sexual reproduction occurs by two main processes — gamete formation and fertilization. In plants it is brought about by pollination followed by double fertilization; in human beings fertilization is internal.** |

Every filled cell comes from the chapter. On the asexual side it says that in asexual reproduction "the new organism has exact genetic similarity with the reproducing organism. This is uniparental reproduction and it occurs by mitotic cell division." On the sexual side it says "Sexual reproduction always occurs with the help of two germ cells. Female gamete and male gamete are those two germ cells", that "Two main processes occur in the sexual reproduction" — "1. Gamete formation: Gametes are formed by the meiosis" and "2. Fertilization: A diploid zygote is formed in this process by union of haploid male and female gametes. The zygote divides by mitosis and embryo is formed."

[Note: the phrase "somatic cells" in the printed row 1 appears nowhere else in the chapter. The chapter's own definition is "Process of formation of new organism by an organism of same species without involvement of gametes is called as asexual reproduction."]

**Testes.**

The chapter states it directly: "Sperms are produced in testes of men from beginning of maturation (puberty) till death." It also describes how — "Testes contain numerous seminiferous tubules. Germinal epithelium present in the tubules divide by meiosis to produce sperms." The testes lie in the scrotum, outside the abdominal cavity.

**Y** chromosome.

The chapter says "X-chromosome is present in men and women whereas Y-chromosome is present in men only", and, in the 'Always remember' box, "if X- chromosomes comes from male, the child will be a girl and if Y-chromosome comes then the child will be a boy." So maleness follows the Y chromosome; the male's sperms are of two kinds, (22 + X) or (22 + Y), while all oocytes are (22 + X).

**Cowper's gland in the male corresponds to Bartholin's gland in the female** — that is the pair of glands the question is pointing at.

What the chapter actually supplies is the two lists, not the equivalence. For the male it names three glands: "Seminal vesicles secrete their secretion in ejaculatory ducts whereas prostate gland and Cowper's glands secrete their secretions in urinogenital duct." For the female it names one: "Besides, a pair of Bartholin's gland is also present." Cowper's gland and Bartholin's gland are the only two that can be set against each other, since the seminal vesicles and the prostate have no counterpart named on the female side.

[Note: the chapter nowhere states that any gland is "the same" in the two systems — it does not use the words same, homologous or equivalent about them, and Bartholin's gland is not labelled on figure 3.17 either. The claim that these two glands correspond therefore does not come from this chapter, and the question's wording is loose: no single gland is literally present in both systems under one name.]

**The uterus** (in its inner lining, the endometrium).

The chapter says of the developing embryo: "Meanwhile, it is pushed towards uterus. Once it reaches the uterus, it is implanted and further development occurs after implantation." The lining is prepared for it in advance — under progesterone "Endometrial glands secrete their secretion... Such endometrium is ready for implantation of embryo.

**Asexual** type of reproduction.

Straight from the chapter's definition: "Process of formation of new organism by an organism of same species without involvement of gametes is called as asexual reproduction. As this reproduction does not involve union of two different gametes, the new organism has exact genetic similarity with the reproducing organism."

**Fragmentation.**

The chapter defines it in almost the same words: "In this type of reproduction, the body of parent organism breaks up into many fragments and each fragment starts to live as an independent new organism. This type of reproduction occurs in algae like Spirogyra, and sponges like Sycon." When Spirogyra has plenty of water and nutrients its filaments grow fast and break into fragments, each growing into a new Spirogyra; and if the body of Sycon breaks up accidentally, "each fragment develops into new Sycon."

**Meiosis** (meiotic cell division).

The chapter gives the general rule under sexual reproduction — "Gamete formation: Gametes are formed by the meiosis. In meiosis, chromosome number is reduced to half; hence haploid gametes are formed" — and states the same thing for the female side of the flower: "Embryo sac is formed in each ovule by meiosis." Pollen grains carry the male gametes ("a long pollen tube and two male gametes are formed"), so they too are products of meiosis and are haploid.

[Note: the chapter does not say this about pollen grains in so many words — the answer is derived from the general gamete rule and the parallel statement about the ovule. The word "locule" used in the question occurs nowhere else in the chapter.]

Completed paragraph (the words supplied are shown in bold):

Growth of follicles present in the ovary occurs under the effect of **follicle stimulating hormone**. This follicle secretes estrogen. **Endometrium of uterus** grows / regenerates under the effect of estrogen. Under the effect of **luteinizing hormone**, fully grown up follicle bursts, ovulation occurs and **corpus luteum** is formed from remaining part of follicle. It secrets **estrogen** and **progesterone**. Under the effect of these hormones, glands of **endometrium of uterus** are activated and it becomes ready for implantation.

The chapter's own account of the menstrual cycle runs in the same order: "One of the several follicles in the ovary starts to develop along with the oocyte present in it, under the effect of follicle stimulating hormone. This developing follicle secretes estrogen. Endometrium of the uterus starts to develop (during first cycle) or regenerate (during subsequent cycles) under the effect of estrogen. Meanwhile, developing follicle completes its development. It bursts under the effect of luteinizing hormone and oocyte is released. This is called as ovulation. Remaining tissue of the burst follicle forms the corpus luteum... Endometrial glands secrete their secretion under the effect of progesterone. Such endometrium is ready for implantation of embryo."

[Note: there are seven blanks but only six words in the bracket — "endometrium of uterus" is needed twice, once as the tissue that regenerates and once as the tissue whose glands are activated. Note also that the chapter's prose names only progesterone as the secretion of the corpus luteum; that it secretes estrogen as well is carried by figure 3.21, which labels the corpus luteum "Progesterone and estrogen", and by the sentence on the next page that when the corpus luteum "transforms into corpus albicans... secretion of estrogen and progesterone stops completely".]

The chapter gives **three** methods of asexual reproduction in unicellular organisms.

**1. Binary fission** — "the parent cell divides to form two similar daughter cells", either by mitosis or by amitosis. It is performed by prokaryotes (bacteria), by protists and even by cell organelles like mitochondria and chloroplasts. The axis of division differs from one protist to another, and the chapter names three examples: **Amoeba** "divides in any plane due to lack of specific shape; hence it is called as 'simple binary fission'", **Paramecium** divides by "transverse binary fission" and **Euglena** by "longitudinal binary fission". It is usually performed in favourable conditions, i.e. when food is abundant.

**2. Multiple fission** — performed by **Amoeba** and similar protists in adverse conditions. Amoeba stops forming pseudopodia, becomes rounded and forms a protective covering around the plasma membrane; such an encysted protist is called a **cyst**. "Many nuclei are formed by repeated nuclear divisions in the cyst. It is followed by cytoplasmic division and thus, many amoebulae are formed." They stay inside until conditions improve, when the cyst bursts open and the amoebulae are released.

**3. Budding** — in **yeast**, a unicellular fungus. The yeast cell "produces two daughter nuclei by mitotic division", a small bulge (the bud) appears on the surface of the parent cell, one of the two daughter nuclei enters the bud, and after enough growth the bud separates and lives independently as a daughter yeast cell.

**IVF is In Vitro Fertilization** — the chapter describes it in one sentence: "In this technique, fertilization is brought about in the test-tube and the embryo formed is implanted in uterus of woman at appropriate time."

It is one of the modern medical techniques by which childless couples can have a child. The chapter gives the cases it is used for: "IVF technique is used for having the child in case of those childless couples who have problems like less sperm count, obstacles in oviduct, etc."

The same technique is the basis of the other two methods the chapter describes. In surrogacy the oocyte "is fertilized in test-tube with the help of sperms collected from her husband" before the embryo is placed in the surrogate mother's uterus; and where a sperm bank is used, "oocyte of woman of the concerned couple is fertilized by IVF technique using the semen from sperm bank." Figure 3.22, "Fertilization in a test tube", shows the ovum with sperms "being introduced through micro needle" while it is held by a micro pipette.

The chapter names the following, and its emphasis is on cleanliness and on awareness rather than on any medical measure.

- **Keep the genitals clean.** For women, "Bleeding occurs during menstrual cycle. Due to this, private organs (genitals) need to be maintained clean time to time, otherwise, problems regarding reproductive health may arise." The chapter puts the same duty on men: "Some problems regarding reproductive health may arise in men too. It is essential to maintain the cleanliness of their genitals."
- **Rest and special personal hygiene during menstruation.** The chapter notes that women "experience severe pains during this period", that "severe weakness is felt due to heavy bleeding" and that "there is higher possibility of infections too during this overall period. Due to all such reasons, there is need of rest along with special personal hygiene."
- **Overcome the lack of awareness.** The chapter blames "various reasons like social customs, traditions, illiteracy, shyness, etc." for the lack of awareness about reproductive health in our country, and says "especially, there seems to be indifference towards the reproductive health of women" — so being informed, and treating women's reproductive health as seriously as men's, is itself a precaution.
- **Be aware of the sexual diseases** the chapter names, syphilis and gonorrhoea, both caused by bacteria, whose symptoms it lists.

[Note: the chapter's "Reproductive health" section is three short paragraphs and prints no numbered list of precautions. Beyond the points above it names none — it says nothing about contraception, medical check-ups, diet or age at marriage, and it does not say how the two sexual diseases are avoided. The only further instruction it gives the student is its own "Get information" box: "Visit a public health center nearby your place and collect the information through an interview of health officer".]

**The menstrual cycle is the set of repetitive changes the female reproductive system undergoes** after puberty. The chapter defines it thus: "Female reproductive system undergoes some changes at puberty and those changes repeat at the interval of every 28 - 30 days. These repetitive changes are called as menstrual cycle."

It is "a natural process, controlled by four hormones. Those four hormones are follicle stimulating hormone (FSH), luteinizing hormone (LH), estrogen and progesterone." In brief, the cycle runs as follows.

1. Under the effect of **FSH**, one of the several follicles in the ovary starts to develop along with the oocyte inside it.
2. The developing follicle secretes **estrogen**, under whose effect the endometrium of the uterus develops (in the first cycle) or regenerates (in later cycles).
3. Under the effect of **LH** the fully grown follicle bursts and the oocyte is released — this is **ovulation**.
4. The remaining tissue of the burst follicle forms the **corpus luteum**, which secretes **progesterone**; the endometrial glands then secrete under its effect and "such endometrium is ready for implantation of embryo."
5. "If oocyte is not fertilized within 24 hours, corpus luteum becomes inactive and transforms into corpus albicans", the secretion of estrogen and progesterone stops, and the endometrium begins to degenerate. "Tissues of degenerating endometrium and unfertilized ovum are discarded out through vagina. This is accompanied with continuous bleeding. Bleeding continues approximately for five days. This is called as menstruation."

The cycle repeats every month "unless the oocyte is fertilized and embryo is implanted. If the embryo is implanted, repetition of this cycle is temporarily stopped till the parturition and thereafter period of breast feeding." It continues from puberty until menopause, when "secretion of hormones controlling the functions of female reproductive system either stops or becomes irregular".

**The statement is explained by the fact that a sexually produced offspring receives genes from both parents.** The chapter puts it plainly: "Fusion of male gamete of male parent and female gamete of female parent occurs. Due to this, new individual always has the recombined genes of both the parents. Hence, the new individual shows similarities with the parents for some characters and has some characters different than both parents."

So the similarity and the difference have the same cause. Gametes are formed by meiosis and are haploid; at fertilization the two haploid sets combine into a diploid zygote, so every character of the new individual is built from a set of genes half of which came from each parent. That is why the child resembles the parents in some characters — and why it is not identical to either of them.

Examples from the chapter:

- **Sex determination.** A child always receives an X chromosome from the mother, and either X or Y from the father: "if X- chromosomes comes from male, the child will be a girl and if Y-chromosome comes then the child will be a boy." The child's sex is thus inherited from the parents, one chromosome from each.
- **Twins.** Monozygotic twins come from a single embryo whose cells divide into two groups, so they carry exactly the same genes: "Such twins are genetically exactly similar to each other. Due to this, such twins are exactly similar in their appearance and their gender is also same." Dizygotic twins come from two separate zygotes formed by two oocytes and two separate sperms, so they are "genetically different and may be same of different by gender." The contrast between the two shows that appearance follows the genes received.

The chapter adds why the differences matter: "Diversity in living organisms occurs due to genetic variation. Genetic variation helps the organisms to adjust with the changing environment and thereby to maintain their existence."

[Note: the chapter gives no list of particular inherited characters (such as eye colour or height) — the two examples above are the ones it actually supplies.]

The diagram to be drawn is the chapter's figure 3.16, "Male reproductive system of human".

**Labels to be shown, exactly as the figure prints them:** Urinary bladder, Seminal vesicle, Prostate gland, Vas deferens, Cowper's gland, Urino genital duct, Epididymis, Scrotum, Ejaculatory duct, Testis, Penis.

**What the drawing shows.** The urinary bladder is at the top, with a seminal vesicle on each side of it and the prostate gland below it. From each testis, held in the scrotum outside the abdominal cavity, the epididymis leads into the vas deferens, which loops up and over the bladder and joins the ejaculatory duct; the ejaculatory duct opens into the urinogenital duct, which runs down the length of the penis. Cowper's gland lies on either side of the urinogenital duct just below the prostate.

**Points from the chapter that the labelled drawing should be consistent with.** "Male reproductive system of humans consists of testes, various ducts and glands. Testes are present in the scrotum, outside the abdominal cavity." The sperms pass through the ducts in this sequence: "rete testis, vas eferens, epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct and urinogenital duct", becoming mature as they are pushed forward. "Seminal vesicles secrete their secretion in ejaculatory ducts whereas prostate gland and Cowper's glands secrete their secretions in urinogenital duct." Also worth remembering while labelling: "All the organs of male reproductive system are paired except urinogenital duct, prostate gland, penis & scrotum" — so the testis, epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct, seminal vesicle and Cowper's gland are each drawn twice, one on each side.

[Note: the answer to this question is the drawing itself. The parts and labels above are listed exactly as the chapter's figure prints them so that the diagram can be reproduced. Two of the chapter's own sequence terms are not labelled on the figure — the rete testis and the "vas eferens" — and the latter is a misprint in the book for vas efferens.]

The diagram to be drawn is the chapter's figure 3.17, "Human female reproductive system".

**Labels shown on the figure:** Oviduct, Ovary, Uterus, Vagina.

**What the drawing shows.** The uterus is the single central organ, drawn in section so that its inner lining is visible; it narrows downward into the vagina. An oviduct runs outward from each upper corner of the uterus and ends in a funnel-like free end close to an ovary, one on each side.

**Points from the chapter the drawing should be consistent with.** "All organs of female reproductive system are in abdominal cavity. It includes a pair of ovaries, a pair of oviducts, single uterus and a vagina. Besides, a pair of Bartholin's gland is also present." The funnel end matters: "Generally, every month, an ovum is released in abdominal cavity alternately from each ovary. Free end of oviduct is funnel-like. An opening is present at the center of it. Oocyte enters the oviduct through that opening. Cilia are present on inner surface of oviduct. These cilia push the oocyte towards uterus."

[Note: the answer to this question is the drawing itself; the four labels above are the ones the chapter's figure carries. Bartholin's gland is named in the text but is NOT labelled on figure 3.17, so it is not part of the printed diagram.]

The diagram to be drawn is the chapter's figure 3.12, "Parts of flower" — a flower cut lengthwise so that both essential whorls are visible.

**Labels shown on the figure:** Corolla (Petals), Calyx (Sepals), Pedicel, Stigma, Style, Ovary, Gynoecium (bracketing stigma + style + ovary), Anther, Filament, Androecium (bracketing anther + filament).

**What the drawing shows.** The pedicel, the stalk, is at the base. Above it the calyx of green sepals, then the corolla of coloured petals, then the stamens, each drawn as a filament carrying an anther at its tip, and at the centre the carpel — a swollen ovary at the base containing ovules, a hollow style rising from it and the stigma at its tip. The stamens together are bracketed as the androecium and the carpel as the gynoecium; these two are the sexual reproductive organs the question asks for.

**Points from the chapter the drawing should be consistent with.** "Flower is structural unit of sexual reproduction in plants. It consists of four floral whorls as calyx, corolla, androecium and gynaecium; arranged in sequence from outside to inside. Androecium and gynoecium are called 'essential whorls' because they perform the function of reproduction whereas calyx and corolla are called as 'accessory whorls' because they are responsible for protection of inner whorls." Also: "Androecium is male whorl and its members are called as stamens. Gynaecium is female whorl and its members are called as carpels... Ovary is present at the basal end of each carpel. A hollow 'style' comes up from the ovary. Stigma is present at the tip of style. Ovary contains one or many ovules."

[Note: the answer to this question is the drawing itself; the labels above are exactly those the chapter's figure prints. The chapter spells the female whorl both "gynaecium" and "gynoecium" in the same passage, and the figure prints "Gynoecium".]

The diagram to be drawn is the chapter's figure 3.21, "Menstrual cycle" — two parallel tracks read left to right against a scale of the 28 days of the cycle.

**Labels shown on the figure:** Pituitary gland; Changes in the ovary during menstruation; Fully grown follicle; Ovulation; Corpus luteum; Corpus albicans; Estrogen; Progesterone and estrogen; changes in the uterus during Menstruation; Period of Menstruation; Period of regeneration of endometrium; Ovulation period; Period of secretions of glands in endometrium; Beginning of new Menstruation.

**What the drawing shows.** The pituitary gland is drawn at the top, with arrows carrying FSH and LH down to the ovary. The upper track shows the ovary: a follicle growing through several stages into a fully grown follicle, then bursting at ovulation, then becoming the corpus luteum and finally the corpus albicans. Arrows mark estrogen coming from the developing follicle and "Progesterone and estrogen" from the corpus luteum, and point down to the lower track. The lower track shows the uterine lining across the same days — shed and bleeding at the start, then regenerating, then thickening with its glands secreting, and finally breaking down again at the beginning of the next menstruation. A numbered day scale from 1 to 28 runs between the two tracks, with the four periods bracketed beneath it.

**The sequence the drawing represents**, from the chapter: a follicle develops under FSH and secretes estrogen; the endometrium regenerates under estrogen; the follicle bursts under LH and ovulation occurs; the remaining tissue forms the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone so the endometrial glands secrete and the endometrium becomes ready for implantation; and "if oocyte is not fertilized within 24 hours, corpus luteum becomes inactive and transforms into corpus albicans", the hormones stop, the endometrium degenerates and menstruation begins again.

[Note: the answer to this question is the drawing itself; the labels above are those the chapter's figure prints. The figure additionally prints "Hypothalamus GnRH" above the pituitary and "FSH" and "LH" inside it — GnRH and the hypothalamus are named nowhere in the chapter's text, only inside this figure.]

**The chapter names no hormone of the male reproductive system.**

It names exactly four hormones in the whole chapter — "follicle stimulating hormone (FSH), luteinizing hormone (LH), estrogen and progesterone" — and it introduces all four as the hormones that control the **menstrual cycle**, that is, the female system. Its section on the human male reproductive system describes the testes, the ducts and the three glands, and mentions no hormone at all.

The chapter does raise the question without answering it: its "Can you recall?" box asks "Which different hormones control the functions of human reproductive system through chemical coordination?" and "Which hormones are responsible for changes in human body occurring during on set of sexual maturity?" — both are put to the student as recall from an earlier class, and neither is answered anywhere in this chapter.

[Note: this answer is deliberately not filled in from general knowledge. The name expected here is not on any page of this chapter.]

**Estrogen and progesterone.**

Both are traced to the ovary in the chapter's account of the menstrual cycle. Estrogen comes from the developing follicle, which lies in the ovary: "One of the several follicles in the ovary starts to develop along with the oocyte present in it, under the effect of follicle stimulating hormone. This developing follicle secretes estrogen." Progesterone comes from the corpus luteum, which is what is left of that follicle after ovulation: "Remaining tissue of the burst follicle forms the corpus luteum. Corpus luteum starts to secrete progesterone."

That the corpus luteum yields both is confirmed twice more: figure 3.21 labels it "Progesterone and estrogen", and the chapter says that once it becomes the corpus albicans, "secretion of estrogen and progesterone stops completely."

**Monozygotic twins and dizygotic twins.** The chapter states it directly: "There are two main types of twins as- monozygotic twins and dizygotic twins."

- **Monozygotic twins** are formed from a single embryo — within 8 days of zygote formation its cells divide into two groups which develop as two separate embryos. "Such twins are genetically exactly similar to each other. Due to this, such twins are exactly similar in their appearance and their gender is also same i.e. both will be either boys or girls."
- **Dizygotic twins** are formed when "two oocytes are released from the ovary of woman and both oocytes are fertilized by two separate sperms and thus two zygotes are formed." Such twins "are genetically different and may be same of different by gender."

The chapter also names **conjoined twins (Siamese twins)** as a special case of the first kind: if the embryonic cells divide into two groups more than 8 days after the zygote is formed, "there is high possibility of formation of conjoined twins (Siamese twins). Such twins are born with some parts of body joined to each other. Some organs are common in such twins."

**Syphilis and gonorrhoea.**

These are the only two the chapter names: "Among the various sexual diseases, syphilis and gonorrhoea occur on large scale. Both of these diseases are caused by bacteria."

It also gives their symptoms. For syphilis: "Occurrence of chancre (patches) on various parts of body including genitals, rash, fever, inflammation of joints, alopecia, etc." For gonorrhoea: "Painful and burning sensation during urination, oozing of pus through penis and vagina, inflammation of urinary tract, anus, throat, eyes, etc."

**The chapter names no method of family planning, and it sends the student out of the book to find them.**

Family planning appears once, as the remedy for population explosion: excessive population growth brings "various problems like unemployment, decreasing per capita income and increasing loan, stress on natural resources, etc. There is only one solution for all such problems and it is population control. Family planning is essential for this."

The methods themselves are set as a task, not taught. The chapter's "Get information" box, printed immediately before this exercise, reads: "Visit a public health center nearby your place and collect the information through an interview of health officer about meaning and various methods of family planning."

[Note: this answer is deliberately not filled in from general knowledge. No method of family planning or contraception is named anywhere in the chapter; the book itself directs the student to a health officer for them.]

**The statement is TRUE.**

The reason is that the two parents do not contribute the same kind of sex chromosome. The chapter sets it out in its "Always remember" box: "The man is totally responsible, whether the couple will have a boy or a girl child. During zygote formation, man contributes either X or Y chromosome to the next generation, but woman contributes only X-sex chromosome to the next generation. At the time of fertilization, if X- chromosomes comes from male, the child will be a girl and if Y-chromosome comes then the child will be a boy."

The chromosome numbers given earlier in the chapter say the same thing. The germ cells are diploid, "22 pairs of autosomes and 1 pair of sex-chromosomes i.e. (44 + XX or 44 + XY)". After meiosis, "Two types of sperms are produced as (22 + X) or (22 + Y) whereas oocytes are produced of only one type as (22 + X)." So the oocyte can supply only an X. Whether the zygote turns out (44 + XX), a girl, or (44 + XY), a boy, is settled entirely by which of the two kinds of sperm fertilizes it — and that comes from the father.

The chapter draws the social conclusion itself: "Thinking of this, is it right to consider the mother responsible for a girl child? We all must take efforts to stop female foeticide."

The chapter describes **two methods of asexual reproduction in plants**, and a third in the algae.

**1. Vegetative propagation.** "Reproduction in plants with the help of vegetative parts like root, stem, leaf and bud is called as vegetative reproduction." The chapter gives three examples: in **potato** it "is performed with the help of 'eyes' present on tuber"; in **Bryophyllum** "it is performed with the help of buds present on leaf margin"; and "in case of plants like **sugarcane & grasses**, vegetative propagation occurs with the help of buds present on nodes." Figure 3.10 also shows the sweet potato.

**2. Spore formation.** "Fungi like **Mucor** have filamentous body. They have sporangia. Once the spores are formed, sporangia burst and spores are released. Spores germinate in moist and warm place and new fungal colony is formed."

**3. Fragmentation**, which the chapter illustrates with an alga: "This type of reproduction occurs in algae like **Spirogyra**, and sponges like Sycon." When there is plenty of water and nutrients, Spirogyra filaments "grow up very fast and break up into many small fragments. Each fragment starts to live independently as a new Spirogyra fiber."

All of these share the features the chapter gives asexual reproduction generally: only one parent is involved, no gametes fuse, division is mitotic, and "the new organism has exact genetic similarity with the reproducing organism". Its drawback is the "absence of genetic recombination" and its advantage is that it is a "fast process".

**The statement is justified, because each of the three techniques answers a different cause of childlessness that the chapter itself lists.**

The chapter first states the problem: "Many couples cannot have children due to various reasons. In case of women, irregularity in menstrual cycle, difficulties in oocyte production, obstacles in the oviduct, difficulties in implantation in uterus and many other reasons are responsible for this. Absence of sperms in the semen, slow movement of sperms, anomalies in the sperms are the reasons in case of males. But now with the help of advanced medical techniques like IVF, Surrogacy, Sperm bank the childless couples can have a child."

- **IVF** answers the case where fertilization cannot happen inside the body: "fertilization is brought about in the test-tube and the embryo formed is implanted in uterus of woman at appropriate time." The chapter names its uses — "childless couples who have problems like less sperm count, obstacles in oviduct, etc."
- **Surrogacy** answers the case where fertilization is possible but implantation is not: "Some women have problems in implantation of embryo in uterus." Her own oocyte is fertilized in a test tube with her husband's sperms, "the embryo formed from such fertilization is implanted in the uterus of some other woman having normal uterus", who is called the surrogate mother. The couple's own gametes are used, so the child is genetically theirs.
- **Sperm bank** answers the case where the male partner cannot supply usable sperms. Semen "ejaculated by the desired men is collected after their thorough physical and medical check-up and stored in the sperm bank", and "as per the wish of needful couple, oocyte of woman of the concerned couple is fertilized by IVF technique using the semen from sperm bank." The chapter records a safeguard too: "Name of the semen donor is strictly kept secret as per the law."

Between them the three techniques therefore cover obstruction of the oviduct, failure of implantation and failure of sperm production — so couples who could not otherwise have a child can have one. That is the sense in which they help human beings.

**In plants, sexual reproduction is carried out by the flower** — "Flower is structural unit of sexual reproduction in plants."

**Structure.** A flower has four whorls arranged from outside inwards: calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium. "Androecium and gynoecium are called 'essential whorls' because they perform the function of reproduction whereas calyx and corolla are called as 'accessory whorls' because they are responsible for protection of inner whorls." The members of the calyx are green sepals and those of the corolla are variously coloured petals. "Androecium is male whorl and its members are called as stamens. Gynaecium is female whorl and its members are called as carpels." Each carpel has an ovary at its base, a hollow style rising from it and a stigma at the tip; the ovary contains one or many ovules. A flower with both essential whorls is **bisexual** (example, **Hibiscus**); one with only a single essential whorl is **unisexual** — male if only the androecium is present, female if only the gynoecium is (example, papaya).

**Gamete formation.** Both gametes are formed by meiosis, so they are haploid. "Embryo sac is formed in each ovule by meiosis. Each embryo sac consists of a haploid egg cell and two haploid polar nuclei." The pollen grains, which carry the male gametes, are produced in the anthers.

**Pollination.** "Pollen grains from anther are transferred to the stigma. This is called as pollination." It is brought about "with the help of abiotic agents (wind, water) and biotic agents (insects and other animals)". Pollination within one flower or between two flowers of the same plant is **self-pollination**; between flowers on two plants of the same species it is **cross-pollination**.

**Double fertilization.** The stigma becomes sticky at pollination, and pollen falling on it germinates: "a long pollen tube and two male gametes are formed. The pollen tube carries male gametes. Pollen tube reaches the embryo sac via style. Tip of the pollen tube bursts and two male gametes are released in embryo sac. One male gamete unites with the egg cell to form zygote. This is fertilization. Second male gamete unites with two polar nuclei and endosperm is formed. As two male nuclei participate in this process, it is called as double fertilization."

**Seed and fruit.** "Ovule develops into seed and ovary into fruit after fertilization. Seeds fall upon the ground when fruits break up and they germinate in the soil under favourable conditions. Zygote develops at the cost of food stored in endosperm of seed and thus a new plantlet is formed. This is called as seed germination."
